rv.q: But this witty and delightful adaptation of the 1984 film A Private Function strikes me as better than the original.
Composer George Stiles and lyricist Anthony Drewe have written a series of charming songs, with nostalgic lilt and literate rhyming that explain the effect Betty Blue Eyes has on stout-hearted men.
A portrait of Britain in an age of austerity and insidious inequalities isn't obvious material for a musical comedy. But it works, cheeringly and at times hilariously.
The show has two aces up its sleeve.

The 1940s cheer us up no end: no sooner have we warmed to the camaraderie of 1941 in Flare Path than we get this romping musical version of 1947: in which two American writers, Ron Cowen and Daniel Lipman, adapt Alan Bennett's tale of snobbery, skulduggery and illegal pig-raising for ‘a private func...
Betty Blue Eyes [is] the most thoroughly English and charming new musical in the West End for a very long time.
I suspect they, like me, may look forward to something rather more meaty.

This likeably performed and technically accomplished musical has some welcome moments that make the audience squeal with laughter, plus a few that may have them grunting impatiently for the next scene to arrive.
